newsitem.title: BELGIUM: CSI sale latest step in EU steel industry upheaval.
newsitem.headline: CSI sale latest step in EU steel industry upheaval.

text.p: The privatisation of Spain's Corporacion Siderurgica Integral (CSI) marks the latest step in a rapid restructuring of Europe's steel industry, not long ago in crisis and needing state money to survive.

The plan by Luxembourg's Arbed to take a 35 percent stake in CSI continues a process which started with the sale of British Steel almost a decade ago and which has left most of the once deeply troubled industry in private hands.
The Spanish government also plans to float between 51 and 65 percent of CSI on the stock exchange this year.
"It is the last thing in a long story of privatisations and mergers," said Dietrich Von Hulsen, director general of the European Confederation of Iron and Steel Industries (Eurofer).

He estimated that about 90 percent of the European Union steel industry, often in trouble since the 1974 oil crisis, was now privately owned. In contrast, as much as 50 to 60 percent of the sector was state controlled only 10 to 15 years ago.
The latest restructuring move coincides with signs that the market situation for steel producers is steadily improving after a sharp fall in output and prices in 1996.
In a report on the sector published last week, the European Commission said output may rise by 6.5 percent to 157 million tonnes this year, boosting profitability.
It even forecast that the decline in jobs should level off in 1997 and 1998, except in Germany and Spain. About 270,000 people work in the industry.

Such a development would further help the sector, which has become more efficient over the last decade by increasing productivity, closing down surplus capacity, and by shedding jobs. It is also making more sophisticated products.
"We have been through tremendous restructuring. That means a lot of rather small companies have been closed down," said an EU steel industry expert.
Von Hulsen said the industry, still sensitive to business cycle swings, was now in a better position to cope with rough times. "We are convinced that the European steel industry is competitive."

Industry analyst Simon Fenwick at investment bank Paribas in London was also positive about the way the industry was developing. "There is certainly some fair way to go but at least things are on the right track now."

In another move this week highlighting the structural changes taking place in the industry, the European Commission approved on Tuesday a venture between German steel giants Thyssen Stahl AG and Krupp Hoesch AG.

The two companies agreed earlier this year to pool their flat steel activities after Krupp's announcement of a hostile takeover of its arch-rival met with fierce resistance of Thyssen workers and German political leaders.
The venture, called Thyssen Krupp Stahl, will become the leading EU supplier of hot-rolled and cold-rolled flat steel, used mainly in the automobile and building industries.
Its main competitors will be other remaining European steel giants, including notably British Steel, France's Usinor Sacilor, Italy's Riva/Ilva, and Arbed.
Although most of the sector is now in private hands, the restructuring is likely to go on, albeit at a slower pace.

"This process will continue but obviously CSI was the last of the major west European producers to go down the privatisation route," said Fenwick at Paribas. "There are still possibilities," said the EU industry expert.
However, not all is well for the sector. Some analysts believe there is still overcapacity in the European market.
Increasing imports from Russia, Ukraine and other ex-Communist countries are also seen as a problem.

"This is a danger for the steel industry in the EU," said Von Hulsen at Eurofer, adding that these producers should reduce capacity but also adapt their production mix, built up during the Cold War era, to the real needs of the market.
